Newly settled spat of Baltic macoma (Macoma balthica) emerge from the egg capsule with a prodissoconch shell measuring just 0.015 cm [Lb = 0.015 cm] in total length, a dimension that reflects the minute propagule size typical of bivalves with planktotrophic larvae. At a controlled temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the eclosion event occurs after an incubation period of 3.0 days [ab = 3.0 days], a brief developmental interval that aligns with the rapid veliger hatching times observed in other tellinid species inhabiting similar intertidal zones. These lecithotrophic individuals are carried by tidal currents before undergoing larval metamorphosis and subsequent settlement onto the soft sediment substrate. Following the exotrophic transition, the post-metamorphic juvenile will commence filter-feeding on phytoplankton. Initial somatic growth is quite rapid as the spat exploits the abundant spring diatom bloom along the Wadden Sea coast, converting available organic matter into calcified shell material and somatic tissue at a pace that sets the stage for the species' well-known ability to dominate mudflat communities in northern European estuaries. The combination of a very small birth size and a short embryonic period allows for high fecundity, enabling populations to persist despite heavy predation pressure from epibenthic crustaceans and wading birds.

As individuals approach the onset of reproductive activity, a characteristic size threshold is reached that signals the transition to maturity. In Baltic macoma, the total length at puberty has been recorded at 1.0 cm [Lp = 1.0 cm], a modest shell dimension that corresponds to an animal roughly in its second year of life when growing under typical North Sea thermal regimes. The dry weight at puberty of 0.0047 grams  represents the minimal body mass necessary to support initial gametogenesis and spawning. Individuals attaining this size divert a portion of their ingested carbon toward gonad development, producing the first cohort of fertilised ova that are then released into the water column. In field populations, the timing of this reproductive milestone is strongly linked to local temperature conditions and food availability. Under moderate thermal conditions of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the time since birth at puberty is 422.0 days [tp = 422.0 days], indicating that pubertal development requires more than a full year following larval settlement. Comparatively, populations inhabiting colder Baltic Sea sites frequently display a delayed schedule, with maturation sometimes postponed until the third growing season.

Maximum shell length in Baltic macoma is limited to an ultimate total length of 2.8 cm [Li = 2.8 cm], a value that distinguishes this species from larger co-occurring bivalves such as Mya arenaria which can exceed 10 cm. The corresponding ultimate dry weight of 0.131 grams  reflects the modest body mass of these tellinids, which allocate most of their somatic energy to shell production rather than to extensive soft-tissue accumulation. Field surveys across the Dutch delta consistently report that individuals exceeding 2.5 cm are rare, and the 2.8 cm benchmark likely represents an asymptotic size approached only under exceptionally favorable conditions of low density and high food supply. Growth increment analysis of annual shell rings reveals that most of the size increase occurs during the first three years, after which the expansion rate decelerates markedly as energy is increasingly redirected toward reproductive output. This pattern of determinate growth, where length stabilises once sexual maturity is achieved, is common among iteroparous bivalves that experience size-dependent predation risk from crabs and flatfish. Survivorship curves for this species indicate that attainment of the ultimate length coincides with the onset of senescence-related physiological deterioration.

Reproductive output in Macoma balthica has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions that mimic the thermal environment of the southern North Sea. An adult measuring 1.64 cm in shell length and maintained at 12 °C [T = 12 °C] produces an average of 158.9 eggs per day [Ri = average of 158.9 eggs per day], corresponding to a reproductive rate at 1.64 cm of 158.9 eggs per day , a substantial daily fecundity that helps offset the high larval mortality characteristic of planktotrophic development. This per-day rate was derived from weekly collections of spawned ova over a complete reproductive season, with each individual depositing multiple egg masses that are fertilised externally in the water column. The temperature dependence of this parameter is noteworthy: experiments conducted at 9 °C produced rates roughly half of those observed at 12 °C, while at 15 °C the output increased further still, though with diminished viability of the released zygotes. The reproductive season in the Wadden Sea typically spans from late March through June, with peak spawning events corresponding to spring phytoplankton blooms that provide essential food for the newly hatched veligers. Such high daily fecundity enables Baltic macoma to rapidly colonise available substrate, ensuring that even when adult densities fluctuate due to winter storms or anoxic events, sufficient recruits are produced to maintain population stability across the intertidal landscape.

Lifespan in Baltic macoma is notably extended for a small-bodied bivalve, with maximum longevity recorded under ambient North Sea temperatures. At 7 °C [T = 7 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is 3832.0 days [am = 3832.0 days], which translates to approximately a decade of life and highlights the species' capacity for slow, sustained growth in cold, resource-limited environments. This remarkable longevity is facilitated by a low resting metabolic rate and the ability to withstand prolonged periods of food scarcity by reducing filtration activity and relying on stored glycogen reserves in the foot muscle. Tagging studies in the Danish Belts have documented individuals surviving through multiple severe winters, emerging each spring to resume feeding and spawning. Senescence in this species manifests as a progressive decline in gonadal output and a thinning of the shell margin, making older individuals more vulnerable to drilling predation by naticid gastropods. The extended post-reproductive period, during which large females continue to contribute eggs but at diminished rates, represents a life-history strategy that buffers populations against recruitment failures in unpredictable years. The species thus integrates a rapid initial embryonic phase, a year-long pubertal delay, and a decade-long adult lifespan into a flexible ontogenetic schedule adapted to the variable thermal regimes of the North Atlantic coastline.
